title: Sequence-cohort pathway stitchbook: percentile synthesis and stitch-trace heuristics
content:
Context:
This is a working note for a slightly different angle on our E2E latency profiling work: instead of just per-stage slice exports, I assembled a stitchable view across sequence cohorts (short/medium/long), cold vs warm KV-cache, and multi-config batching regimes. The goal is to produce a compact p50/p95/p99 synthesis that can be used by SRE/Perf to choose targeted mitigations (e.g., adaptive batching thresholds, KV warming heuristics).

TL;DR:
- Synthesis aggregates traces by sequence-length cohorts and request ancestry (cold-start vs warm, with/without prior prefix cache).
- Key hotspots differ dramatically by cohort: tokenization/parse dominates short sequences; attention-kernel compute dominates long sequences; batching wait is the wildcard at p95/p99 under bursty arrival.
- Proposed quick fixes: (1) short-seq fast-path that bypasses heavy tokenization hooks, (2) KV-cache prefetcher for 2–4 token prefixes on dedicated pools, (3) microburst admission control with fast-fallback to priority lanes.

Instrumentation and stitch rules:
- Stage instrumentation mapping used for this doc (names are the canonical telemetry tags):
  - ingress_recv_ms (client->front proxy)
  - parse_and_tokenize_ms (tokenizer + preprocessing hooks)
  - route_and_auth_ms (routing + api-key checks)
  - batch_wait_ms (time spent queued in batcher)
  - kv_lookup_ms (distributed KV hits/misses, including network RTT)
  - model_forward_ms (pure model kernel execution on GPU)
  - kv_store_ms (writing any new prefix values, async)
  - decode_emit_ms (post-processing, detokenization, filters)
  - egress_send_ms (front-proxy->client)

- Stitch heuristic: group traces by request_id and parent_request_id (for user streams) and collapse repeated stage pairs where duration < 2ms (noise). Mark traces with cold_kv_tag if kv_lookup_ms includes a remote_miss label.

Sampling and cohorts:
- Data window: 72 hours (2026-02-28 -> 2026-03-02) sampled at 1k traces/sec overall and weighted sampling for p99-eligible long sequences (oversample 10x sequences > 512 tokens).
- Cohorts: short (<=32 tokens), medium (33–512), long (>512). Also separate cold_kv vs warm_kv within each cohort.

Synthesis table (p50/p95/p99) — median milliseconds per stage (cohort-level summary):

Short cohort (<=32 tokens, N=120k):
  p50: ingest 4 | parse 12 | route 3 | batch_wait 1 | kv_lookup 2 | model_forward 18 | decode 6 | egress 3  => total ~49ms
  p95: ingest 6 | parse 40 | route 4 | batch_wait 8 | kv_lookup 8 | model_forward 28 | decode 12 | egress 5 => total ~111ms
  p99: ingest 12 | parse 220 | route 8 | batch_wait 60 | kv_lookup 42 | model_forward 50 | decode 40 | egress 10 => total ~442ms
  Notes: p99 dominated by pathological parse/tokenizer time (complex punctuation + large user prompt attachments) and batching spikes.

Medium cohort (33–512 tokens, N=90k):
  p50: ingest 5 | parse 28 | route 4 | batch_wait 2 | kv_lookup 6 | model_forward 95 | decode 22 | egress 5 => total ~167ms
  p95: ingest 8 | parse 110 | route 5 | batch_wait 12 | kv_lookup 22 | model_forward 180 | decode 45 | egress 8 => total ~390ms
  p99: ingest 16 | parse 420 | route 12 | batch_wait 90 | kv_lookup 85 | model_forward 380 | decode 120 | egress 18 => total ~1,141ms
  Notes: model_forward becomes dominant at p95/p99; batch_wait still contributes heavily when burst factor > 1.5x provisioned.

Long cohort (>512 tokens, N=8k, oversampled):
  p50: ingest 6 | parse 60 | route 8 | batch_wait 4 | kv_lookup 34 | model_forward 760 | decode 140 | egress 12 => total ~1,024ms
  p95: ingest 10 | parse 180 | route 12 | batch_wait 18 | kv_lookup 120 | model_forward 1,620 | decode 320 | egress 20 => total ~2,320ms
  p99: ingest 18 | parse 600 | route 20 | batch_wait 240 | kv_lookup 480 | model_forward 3,150 | decode 860 | egress 45 => total ~5,413ms
  Notes: long sequences amplify model-forward and decode. KV misses cascade (remote lookup per-chunk) — see hypotheses below.

Cold vs Warm KV split (medium cohort p95):
  - warm_kv (70%): total ~320ms (model_forward 160, kv_lookup 8)
  - cold_kv (30%): total ~520ms (model_forward 170, kv_lookup 80)
  Observation: cold_kv increases tail by ~200ms and correlates with multi-chunk remote fetches.

Representative trace snippets (abbreviated):
- Short p99 example (trace id T-20260301-9a7):
  ingest 14 -> parse 210 -> route 6 -> batch_wait 72 -> kv_lookup 38 (remote_miss) -> model_forward 46 -> decode 36 -> egress 10
  Hypothesis: tokenizer pipeline hit pathological regex fallback caused by user prompt with embedded JSON and long base64 chunk.

- Medium p99 example (trace id T-20260302-c14):
  ingest 18 -> parse 420 -> route 8 -> batch_wait 94 -> kv_lookup 86 -> model_forward 376 -> decode 120 -> egress 19
  Hypothesis: combination of batch coalescing with one slow KV lookup created a convoy effect inside the batcher.

- Long p99 example (trace id T-20260301-d88):
  ingest 22 -> parse 540 -> route 18 -> batch_wait 236 -> kv_lookup 488 (3 remote chunks) -> model_forward 3,150 -> decode 860 -> egress 45
  Hypothesis: multi-chunk streaming requests triggering repeated remote fetches; model kernels experience GPU contention due to oversubscription.

Key hypotheses (ranked):
1) Tokenization pathological cases are high-impact at p99 for short and medium cohorts; mitigations: faster fallback, regex-timeout, safe-parser sandbox.
2) Batch wait coupling with outlier KV latency causes convoy. If one request in batch has large kv_lookup_ms, it drags the whole batch. Mitigation: isolate or prefetch KV; make batcher tolerant to pairwise outliers (early release for fast members).
3) Remote KV misses for long sequences are often multi-chunk; network roundtrips are serialized per-chunk. Mitigation: parallelized chunk fetch and local merge/stream assembly.
4) GPU kernel degradation at high concurrency due to sequence-length variance; mitigation: sequence bucketing at scheduler level or based on dynamic sequence-length aware packing.

Experimental ideas to validate quickly:
- Run a small A/B on production traffic (10% traffic) enabling a tokenizer timeout and defaulting to a light-tokenizer for inputs >20% non-ascii. Instrument p99 tokenization time and error rates. (JIRA-ENG-5722)
- Implement a batcher opt-in flag that allows early-responders: if N_fast >= 80% after X ms, flush the batch for them and schedule stragglers separately. Microbench with QPS replay.
- KV prefetch probe: for multi-chunk requests, fetch next chunk prefixes in parallel with model-forward for current chunk (simulate with recorded traces).

Actionable next steps / playbook items:
- Short-term (1–2 wks): add tokenization backstop with timeout + fallback; add telemetry tag that surfaces "tokenizer-fallback-triggered". Owner: Evan.
- Mid-term (3–6 wks): prototype batcher early-release logic and a KV-prefetcher on the dedicated pool. Owner: Marina.
- Long-term (quarter): scheduler-level sequence bucketing and kernel selection improvement to reduce p99 model-forward variance. Owner: Diego / runtime team.

Open questions / notes to investigate:
- Are all tokenizer p99 cases user-caused (malformed inputs) or do we have an internal regex explosion? Need sample corpus and a deterministic reproducer.
- Where is the KV lookup backlog originating? Is it network (host-level) or remote store slowness? Need server-side tcpdump and metrics for remote-store P99 latency.
- How often do we see batcher convoy vs single-request KV outlier? Preliminary ratio ~3:1 (convoy:single) in medium cohort, but needs better sampling.

Slack / PR context:
- Slack thread: #perf-traces -> thread ts 1643XXXX (see linked_artifacts).
- Related PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/3186 (batcher telemetry + stage tags).

Notes to self (scratch):
- Keep this doc light — goal is a concise synthesis for SRE cadence. Will iterate into a more formal playbook after validating tokenizer fixes on canary.
- Save sampled p99 traces to s3://perf-archive/2026-03-seq-cohort-sample for offline replay.

Appendix — quick checklist for on-call when alerted for p99 spikes:
  1) Check cohort histogram for recent 10m window (short/medium/long).
  2) Look at batcher queue depth and batch sizes (if mean batch size > configured + 20%, suspect coalescing).
  3) Inspect kv-store p95/p99 for remote-store AND local LRU evictions.
  4) If tokenizer p99 triggered, capture raw input (redact PII) and file a reproducer.

End of draft.

Feedback welcome — particularly from runtime and tokenizer owners.
